sources.headline: Trump calls GDP data released before midterms ‘fake’, demands investigation
sources.text: President says it was a deliberate decision to release ‘fake’ growth numbers before US midterm elections.United States President Donald Trump has accused his Department of Commerce of purposely issuing incorrect economic growth figures before the midterm elections and says he wants to launch an investigation.Trump made his comments on Thursday when offices and stock markets were closed for the Thanksgiving holiday.Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Talarico wins Senate race, ending decades of Republican dominance in Texaslist 2 of 4Democrats deliver a historic rout to Republicans in US midtermslist 3 of 4US petrol prices are down, but elevated inflation continueslist 4 of 4US voters want Democrats focused on ending Iran war, lowering costs: Pollend of listThe US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis on Wednesday revised third-quarter annualised growth up to 4.3 percent from the advance estimate of 3.4 percent it announced on October 29. Trump’s Republican Party suffered heavy losses in the November 3 elections.“It was just revealed that the REAL Numbers on the Economy, published before the Election, were FAKE,” Trump said in a Truth Social post without providing evidence for the accusation.“Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation. This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error,” he said.Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine trust in economic data that fail to match his claims of a historic boom, a pattern that threatens the credibility of figures needed by businesses, financial markets and consumers when making investments.The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) routinely updates its economic data to improve their accuracy. Gross domestic product (GDP) figures, monthly jobs reports and other data are regularly revised. Those updates occur on a prescheduled basis without regard to the political calendar.The BEA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It has previously said GDP estimates can differ from the final numbers because advance estimates for quarterly growth lack complete source data on inventories, trade and consumer spending on services.A May article coauthored by BEA Director Vipin Arora found that for GDP, the estimates released 90 days after initial estimates typically differed by 0.52 percentage points throughout this century.“That is, over these 25 years, more complete source data expanded or contracted BEA’s estimates of real GDP growth on average by about half a percentage point per quarter,” wrote Arora and coauthor Rebecca Pocase.Last year, Trump fired a top Department of Labor official after a weak jobs report, accusing her without evidence of manipulating the figures, a move that added to already growing concerns about the quality of economic data published by the federal government.

Trump calls GDP figures ‘fake’, demands probe of his own Commerce Department

The US president claimed bad data was purposefully released, linking it to his party’s poor performance in the recent midterm elections

Associated Press
Published: 1:06am, 27 Nov 2026

US President Donald Trump on Thursday accused his Commerce Department of purposely issuing incorrect economic growth figures before the midterm elections and said he wants to launch an investigation.

Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine trust in economic data that fails to match his claims of a historic boom, a pattern that threatens the credibility of figures needed by businesses, financial markets and consumers when making investments.

His latest complaint concerns data issued by the Commerce Department on Wednesday that revised gross domestic product in the third quarter to 4.3 per cent on an annual basis, up from a prior estimate of 3.4 per cent.

The department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis routinely updates its economic data to improve its accuracy. GDP figures, monthly jobs reports and other data are regularly revised. Those updates occur on a pre-scheduled basis without regard to the political calendar.

But the president claimed on social media that it was a “massive, and purposeful, error” and linked it to the poor performance for Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections that gave Democrats control of both houses of Congress.

02:33

“It was just revealed that the REAL Numbers on the Economy, published before the Election, were FAKE, and a correction was issued yesterday by the people in the Government Agency that does these numbers,” Trump posted.

“Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation.”

The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The government is largely closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday.

This is the latest instance of Trump questioning the integrity of economic data he feels is unfavourable to him without providing evidence that revisions are politically motivated.

In August 2025, Trump fired the head of the Bureau of Labour Statistics after a decidedly weak jobs report. That report said only 73,000 jobs were added in July 2025 and showed that 258,000 fewer jobs were added in May and June than previously reported.

Trump called that jobs report “phony” and “rigged”.

Trump has claimed that he deserves credit for powering stronger economic growth, but voters do not share the president’s belief that the economy is strong.

In the midterms, 76 per cent described economic conditions as “not so good” or “poor”, according to the AP Voter Poll, an extensive survey of the electorate. About two-thirds of voters said Trump’s own policies had fuelled inflation.

The president in his social media post ignored that the same federal agency on Wednesday also reported that a key measure of inflation – the personal consumption expenditures price index – accelerated to an annual pace of 3.8 per cent in October.

sources.headline: Trump calls for investigation into ‘fake’ US GDP figures
sources.text: WEST PALM BEACH, United States - President Donald Trump called on Nov 26 for an investigation into a routine revision of economic growth figures as he pushed his groundless claims of interference in the US midterm elections.Trump lashed out at what he called “FAKE” figures a day after the US Commerce Department strongly revised GDP growth in the third quarter up to 4.3% from the previous estimate of 3.4%.Such updates are commonplace.“Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation,” Trump said, on his Truth Social network.“This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error.”Trump followed up in a lengthy second post for the US Thanksgiving holiday in which he also took aim at a series of perceived enemies and critics of his extensive makeover of the White House.“I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late,” wrote Trump.He added that it was a “RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated.”Trump’s allegation of deliberate action echoes his other recent baseless claims calling into doubt his Republican Party’s brutal defeat in the Nov 3 midterm elections.Democrats won control of Congress as voters hammered Trump’s Republicans over economic headwinds sparked by the Iran war and the president’s chaotic tariff policies.Throughout his two presidencies, the 80-year-old Trump has repeatedly attacked the political, legal and economic norms that have long underpinned US democracy.Trump has previously defended his economic performance by pointing to data like GDP growth, which has been robust despite the headwinds, mainly on the back of the AI boom.Issuing its new GDP estimate on Nov 25, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis said the growth “primarily reflected an acceleration in investment and an upturn in government spending that were partly offset by a downturn in exports.” AFP
